tx.t: In today's lecture, I will talk about the growth of cities. In two thousand and seven, for the first time in history, more than half of the world's people lived in cities.
The United Nations expects the figure to reach about two thirds by twenty fifty. Cities take up only about two per cent of the Earth's land, but they produce most of the world's wealth.

tx.t: In this talk I would like to tell the story of chocolate. Chocolate comes from the seeds of the cacao tree, which first grew in Central and South America.

The Maya and the Aztecs drank a bitter chocolate drink, often with chilli, and sometimes used the beans as money. Spanish explorers brought cacao to Europe in the sixteenth century, and people began to add sugar.
The first solid eating chocolate was made by an English company, Fry, in eighteen forty-seven. Milk chocolate was invented by a Swiss man, Daniel Peter, in eighteen seventy-five.

The scheme soon met a serious problem: theft and damage. The council solved it with a tracking system fixed inside each frame.

It stretches for roughly two thousand three hundred kilometres. It is not one reef but a network of nearly three thousand individual reefs.

More than one thousand five hundred species of fish live there, together with many kinds of turtles and sharks. Warm water causes corals to expel the algae that feed them, which turns them white. This is called bleaching.

tx.t: Today we are going to look at Antarctica, the coldest continent. About ninety-eight per cent of Antarctica is covered in ice.

The lowest temperature ever recorded on Earth, minus eighty-nine degrees Celsius, was measured there at Vostok Station in nineteen eighty-three. The ice contains about seventy per cent of the world's fresh water.

No people are native to Antarctica. Only scientists live there, and their numbers change with the seasons. The Antarctic Treaty of nineteen fifty-nine, signed by twelve countries, says that the continent can be used only for peaceful purposes and science.

items.title: Ulugh Beg and the Samarkand Observatory

tx.t: Today I would like to tell you about Ulugh Beg, the ruler and astronomer of Samarkand. Ulugh Beg was a grandson of the conqueror Timur, and he ruled Samarkand in the first half of the fifteenth century.
He built a great observatory in Samarkand in the fourteen twenties. Its main instrument was a giant sextant, with a radius of about forty metres.
With it, his team made a catalogue of more than a thousand stars that was used for centuries. His measurement of the length of the year was wrong by less than a minute.
